title: POC Weekly - Latency Tuning (Rivermark)
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on latency tuning. Reviewed TTFT regressions with new streaming patch, sequence length profiles, and kernel selection impacts. Agreed to run two new benchmarks (512 vs 1024 seq) with batching profiles and enable prefix cache. Next: Redwood to share updated benchmark sheet, enable streaming flags on dedicated cluster, customer to run internal traffic-shaped test by next week.
topics: kernel selection — cuBLAS vs FlashAttention vs Triton
batching, KV cache and warmup effects
next_steps: Redwood: share updated benchmark spreadsheet and raw traces (by 2027-04-22)
Rivermark: run traffic-shaped test with streaming enabled (by 2027-04-28)
Joint: schedule kernel-level triage meeting if TTFT doesn't improve (week of 2027-04-26)
action_items: Samira Patel: upload benchmark sheet + notes to shared drive (due 2027-04-22)
Diego Morales: enable streaming flags and run basic 512/1024 comparison on dedicated cluster (due 2027-04-23)
Priya Singh: provide representative request distributions and 95th perc seq lengths (due 2027-04-22)
Tom Hargrove: run traffic-shaped client test and share results (due 2027-04-28)
transcript:
[00:00] Samira: Alright everyone, thanks for jumping on. Trying to keep this to 45. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Tom: Tom Hargrove here. 
[00:08] Priya: Priya Singh. 
[00:09] Ellen: Ellen Park, hi. 
[00:11] Diego: Diego Morales from Redwood. Samira: Samira Patel. Cool.
[00:20] Samira: Goal for today's sync is to review the latency numbers from last week's patch, do a short triage on TTFT, and agree on the next bench runs.
[00:28] Tom: Sounds good. We saw an uptick in time to first token on streaming configs when we pushed the new kernel, about plus 25 to 40 ms on average, higher on cold requests.
[00:36] Diego: Right, that's the thing we wanted to dig into — the patched FlashAttention integration plus Triton kernel fallback path may be adding extra scheduling overhead.
[00:46] Priya: To add context, most of our calls are 150–400 tokens, 95th perc hits around 520, but we also have a small long tail up to 1k. So the mix matters.
[00:58] Samira: Good, so sequence length distribution is consistent with what we saw. Diego, can you run through the specific numbers from your bench?
[01:06] Diego: Sure. I ran three profiles on the dedicated pool: baseline (cuBLAS kernels, no streaming), patched FlashAttention enabled streaming, and a Triton fallback path with batching. For 512 seq avg, baseline TTFT median ~95ms, patched streaming median ~120ms, Triton fallback ~140ms. For 1024 seq median baseline ~170ms, patched streaming ~210ms. Note these are cold-ish measurements — no warm KV cache.
[01:35] Tom: Those match roughly what we saw. The thing that concerns our infra team is the cold start especially when requests hit a GPU that hasn't warmed.
[01:43] Diego: Yep. A few hypotheses: 1) streaming path adds an extra micro-batching scheduler layer, 2) FlashAttention launch cost can be higher on first kernel invocation, 3) Triton fallback incurs kernel launch and marshalling overhead.
[01:57] Priya: Is there any way to keep TTFT low for cold requests? We can't keep all GPUs warm 24/7.
[02:02] Samira: Two levers — smarter warmup heuristics (light weight synthetic prepops) and prefix/KV caching for common prompts. Also we can tune the streaming chunk size so the first chunk returns earlier. Diego, we had flagged chunk size 32 vs 64 earlier?
[02:16] Diego: Correct. In our experiments smaller chunk size (32 tokens) reduced TTFT by ~15ms because we return the first token faster, but it slightly increased overall throughput due to more frequent kernel ops. There's a tradeoff.
[02:29] Ellen: For our product the first token latency is very visible, users complain even if the tail is fine. So we want the lowest TTFT possible. Cost is secondary but still important.
[02:39] Tom: Also want to call out quantization profile — we're on q4f16 for the model, if we move to int8/4-bit we might change kernel choices. Any comments?
[02:48] Diego: Quantization interacts with kernel selection. FlashAttention has good support for certain data types, but Triton kernels can be more flexible for lower-bit inference, though quantized kernels may increase per-token time if memory access patterns aren't optimal. We can run a q8 bench.
[03:03] Samira: Ok so concrete bench plan: 512 vs 1024 seq, streaming chunk 32 vs 64, kernels cuBLAS/FlashAttention/Triton, batching 1/4/8, with warm vs cold cache. Diego, can you enumerate what you'll run?
[03:14] Diego: I'll do a matrix: seqLen {512,1024}, chunk {32,64}, kernel {cuBLAS, FA, Triton}, batch {1,4,8}, cache {cold,warm}. That is 2x2x3x3x2 = 72 runs. Each run will be 5k requests to get stable medians and 95th perc. Expect to finish on dedicated cluster in ~24 hours.
[03:33] Priya: If it's 24 hours we can wait for results. Also we can provide our traffic-shaped generator to match real distribution.
[03:39] Samira: Perfect. Tom, you mentioned traces earlier — can you share a couple of raw request traces?
[03:44] Tom: Yes, we'll dump them to the shared drive tonight.
[03:47] Diego: One more note — the streaming patch had a small bug where the scheduler waits for first micro-batch ack before returning; we patched that but maybe not all paths are hot. I'm going to enable an aggressive path that returns token as soon as decoder outputs available, but it could slightly increase CPU overhead on the host.
[04:03] Priya: Fine with that if TTFT improves.
[04:06] Ellen: What's the impact on cost? More CPU overhead — are we billed differently?
[04:10] Samira: For Dedicated, the cost is mostly GPU-hours; small CPU delta won't change billing but might affect our capacity calculations. We'll surface any noticeable cost delta in the bench sheet.
[04:19] Tom: Also curious about prefix cache. For many of our prompts the first 20–30 tokens are identical. Could enabling prefix/KV cache reduce TTFT dramatically?
[04:28] Diego: Yes, prefix cache helps a lot for repeated prefixes — TTFT can drop because KV fetch is much cheaper than recompute. But cache hit rates depend on prompt variability; Priya, do you have numbers on prefix reuse?
[04:37] Priya: Roughly 45% of requests share a common lead-in prompt, 30% are slightly modified, 25% are free-form. So cache would help a good chunk.
[04:45] Diego: Great. I'll include cache-on vs cache-off runs in the matrix.
[04:50] Samira: Any blockers on running these?
[04:52] Priya: We need to schedule a maintenance window if you hit our staging cluster, but for your dedicated infra it's fine. We also need to confirm TLS cert rotation windows.
[04:59] Samira: Noted. We'll avoid forced restarts during your maintenance window.
[05:03] Tom: One more question — on the Triton side you mentioned marshalling overhead, can we pipeline marshalling with transfers to hide latency?
[05:10] Diego: In principle yes, but requires a small runtime change; we can do a pipeline where host-to-device copy and kernel launch are overlapped for subsequent micro-batches. That will reduce TTFT for batched requests, but for batch=1 benefits are limited.
[05:23] Samira: Okay. If TTFT doesn't get to target we'll schedule a kernel triage with our runtime team.
[05:29] Ellen: What's our TTFT target?
[05:31] Tom: We want median under 80ms for typical 512 seq, and 95th under 200ms.
[05:36] Samira: Got it. We'll aim for that.
[05:39] Diego: To recap actions: I'll run the matrix, enable the aggressive streaming return path, test prefix cache, and run q8 sample. Samira will upload bench sheet and notes. Rivermark will run traffic-shaped test.
[05:51] Priya: We'll also give you updated token distribution and the maintenance windows.
[05:55] Samira: Great. Any other items?
[05:58] Tom: No, thanks team.
[06:00] Samira: Thanks all, we'll sync same time next week unless we need the kernel triage sooner.
[06:06] Diego: Bye everyone.
[06:08] [call end]
